participation.text: Imperial standards expressed central requirements; local officials made practical choices.

evidence.text: Inscribed measures document announced standards; administrative documents let researchers test practice.

coordination.text: Officials, writing-surface makers and recorded recipients connected standards with recurring administrative work. Local variation and coerced labor require their own evidence.

name: Qin: a standard and its everyday use
place: Qin imperial administration; local evidence at Liye, Hunan, China
geographicPrecision: Liye administrative-document site, not an imperial capital or a reconstructed boundary.

interval.label: Imperial Qin frame, 221–206 BCE
interval.note: Met convention; National Palace Museum and the administrative study use 221–207 BCE. This is a period convention, not an exact date for every surviving object or document.

alternatives.label: 221–207 BCE in the National Palace Museum label and Staack’s study; this atlas uses the Met’s 221–206 BCE convention.

question: Does an imperial standard mean everyone followed it in the same way?
summary: An imperial standard needed people, materials and repeated work to become ordinary practice. Qin measuring objects announced central authority, while excavated wooden records show officials processing grain, reports and responsibilities in a conquered region. These sources let us compare what a government required with how an office worked. They preserve both coordination and constraint without making every official, worker or household identical.

sections.title: A common rule travelled on different devices
sections.text: A balance weight compares mass; a capacity measure holds volume. Either could carry an imperial decree while doing a different job. The Palace Museum dates its measure’s decree to the First Emperor’s 26th year, 221 BCE. The text announces conquest, imperial title and common standards, with peace as a royal claim. An inscribed decree did not prove accuracy in every transaction.

sections.title: A local office had to make records usable
sections.text: At Liye, excavated wood documents are associated with Qianling county administration and date mainly to 222–208 BCE. Officials wrote, received and annotated records. Staack compares actual tablets with prescriptions about size and writing layout, and studies tallies used when grain was issued. Reliable recording required the relevant facts to remain identifiable even when their arrangement varied. This was practical work: preparing writing surfaces, recording responsibility and keeping information available for another official to process or check.

sections.title: Making the writing surface was work too
sections.text: The paper connects the collection and preparation of wood with legal provisions and a fragment recording a person cutting tablets. It suggests that some stationery could have been made by assigned convict labor. That proposal matters because an archive depended on more people than the named scribes. The fragment does not identify the maker of every surviving tablet, and the labor arrangement remains a qualified reconstruction. Officials’ choices about materials and time should therefore be read alongside the unequal power that organized work.

citations.locator: Printed p. 157, wood preparation and qualified convict-labor interpretation

sections.title: Uniformity had practical limits
sections.text: Lengths and required information were more consistent than some widths or layouts. Staack proposes practical reasons: compatible documents were easier to handle, while using narrower wood or more writing could save resources. These are explanations tested against a local archive, not proof that every departure was resistance or every office enjoyed the same freedom. Even fines did not guarantee identical documents. The contrast between prescribed form and observed practice makes standardization a historical process that needs investigation.

claims.text: Liye documents show uneven adherence to prescribed document standards; the study does not establish identical practice throughout the empire.

returnPrompt: Which feature of a local document would help distinguish a workable adaptation from a failure to record responsibility?

deeperReading.title: The comparison uses sources with different histories
deeperReading.text: The Liye records come from excavation; the Yuelu Academy manuscripts used for some prescribed formats were not archaeologically excavated. Staack explicitly says their exact provenance is unclear. Their contents and comparison with excavated material inform his argument, but they must not acquire a secure Liye findspot by being discussed beside that archive. The regional map locates the capital, Liye and the royal mausoleum; it does not mark Yuelu Academy as an ancient source location. A next inquiry should examine the relevant legal manuscripts and archaeological publications in greater detail.

deeperReading.title: One archive gives a local test, not a census
deeperReading.text: The study’s measured subsets depend on preservation and on what had been published with usable photographs. The differences it finds cannot be projected automatically to every Qin county. Even a named scribe’s preferred arrangement does not reveal all of that person’s training or choices. The author considers shortages of qualified staff and differing backgrounds as possible explanations. Following those questions requires additional archives and labor evidence, including people whose work produced records but who did not write an account of their own. Qin’s short imperial interval is also distinct from the longer history of the state and its projects.

evidenceReading.title: Compare an announcement, a prescription and a record
evidenceReading.introduction: The passages below are paraphrases of the museum accounts and Staack’s research, not newly translated Qin inscriptions.

items.label: A decree makes a claim
items.text: The inscribed capacity measure announces a common standard after conquest and the assumption of an imperial title.
items.interpretation: This is evidence for a royal announcement attached to a device. A balance weight and a capacity measure are different objects, and neither measures universal compliance.

items.label: Provenance belongs to each manuscript group
items.text: Liye documents were excavated; the Yuelu Academy manuscript collection used for some regulations is unprovenanced.
items.interpretation: Do not identify the regulation as an excavated Liye tablet or use the modern institution’s location as an ancient findspot.

items.label: Variation has more than one possible explanation
items.text: Staack finds differences in material dimensions and arrangement alongside relatively stable required information.
items.interpretation: His proposed pragmatic explanations are not a verdict on every official or on administration throughout the empire.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded C3 explanation with main/deeper/evidence reading, family entry, distinct reference phases and sourced geographic orientation.
limitations: The 27-page Staack paper was downloaded; specified sections, tables and source images were consulted, not every referenced Chinese edition.
Some regulations derive from the unprovenanced Yuelu collection. Household experience, recruitment and the scale of coerced work need more evidence.
No newly licensed photograph of an inscribed measure was added; the graphic is a modern comparison guide.

placeStudy.title: Qin: a capital, a royal project and a county archive
placeStudy.description: Three approximate locators distinguish institutions at different scales. Liye is the excavated archive site; Xianyang is the capital orientation and the Lishan tomb a separate royal project. No imperial boundary, road or movement of a particular document is reconstructed.

points.label: Xianyang — capital orientation
points.text: UNESCO relates the mausoleum’s layout to the Qin capital Xianyang. This is a broad capital-area locator, not a surveyed palace precinct.

points.label: Lishan — royal mausoleum
points.text: The mausoleum project began before the imperial case window. A tomb’s material program and the work of an administrative county archive are different evidence.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: location and project chronology

points.label: Liye / Qianling — excavated records
points.text: Documents recovered at Liye are associated with Qianling county. They offer a local test of practice, not a sample of every office across the empire. The unprovenanced Yuelu collection is not assigned this findspot.
